chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Bureyd al-Ijli, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman, so her sister escorted her to him, and she was older than her. So she entered the house of her husband at night, and she went to the clothes of his wife, removed them from her, and wore them. Then she sat in the room of her sister, and she pushed aside his wife, and extinguished the lamp, and the girl was shy to speak.

So the husband entered the room and had intercourse with her, while he thought that she was his wife whom he had married. So when it was morning, the man's wife stood up to him and said to him, 'I am your so-and-so wife whom you married, and my sister plotted against me, so she took my clothes and wore them, and sat in the room, and pushed me aside.'
So the man investigated that matter and found it as she had mentioned.

So he (peace be upon him) said: 'I view that there is no dower for the one who deceived herself, and I view the legal punishment upon her for what she did, the punishment of the unmarried adulteress. And the husband should not approach his wife whom he married until the waiting period of the one who deceived herself expires. So when her waiting period expires, he joins his wife to him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling when a woman's sister impersonates her to consummate the marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'ghurur' (deception) in marriage contracts, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the validity of the union and the rights of the parties. The ruling emphasizes that while the husband's consummation with the impersonator is valid due to his reasonable belief, the sister incurs the hadd punishment for zina (adultery) as an unmarried woman and forfeits her dower, while the actual wife remains in a state of separation until her 'iddah concludes. This case highlights the importance of clear identification in marital relations and the legal consequences of mistaken identity in classical fiqh.
